note: Rav Avya came to Rava's house with clay on his feet and put them on the bed. Rava grew angry and set out to torment him with hard questions: why may a naphtha lamp be moved on Shabbat? Rav Avya said it can be used to cover a vessel. Rava objected that then every pebble in the yard could be moved too. Rav Avya answered that a lamp has the status of a vessel and pebbles do not, citing a baraita on jewelry and Ulla's reason for it. Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: Thank God that Rava did not embarrass Rav Avya.
why: Rabba and Rav Yosef have just ruled, against Rav Yehuda, that even a naphtha lamp may be moved on Shabbat; Rava's challenge asks for their reason, and Rav Avya supplies it.

note: A man's wife died and left him a nursing baby, and he could not afford to pay a wet-nurse. A miracle happened: he grew breasts like a woman's and nursed his son himself. Rav Yosef said this showed how great the man was, that such a miracle was done for him; Abaye answered that, on the contrary, it showed how lowly he was, that the order of creation had to be changed for him. Rav Yehuda drew a different lesson: feeding a person is so hard that nature itself was altered, and Rav Naḥman added that miracles do happen, but food has never been created by one.
why: The Gemara has been discussing whether goats may go out on Shabbat with pouches on their udders, and has just told of goats in Antioch with huge udders; it attaches this related baraita about a miracle of nursing.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Talmud discusses.

note: The Sages told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that young children had come to the study hall and said things not heard even in the days of Joshua bin Nun. Going through the Hebrew alphabet, they read the letters as lessons: alef-beit means 'learn wisdom', gimmel-dalet means 'give to the poor', and the gimmel's leg reaches toward the dalet because the generous run after the poor. They read the open and closed forms of letters as open and hidden teachings, and as humble righteous people who will one day be known, and the shapes of kuf and reish as God turning from the wicked while leaving an opening through which he can return.
why: The Gemara has been discussing the open and closed forms of letters such as mem and samekh and how old those forms are; the children's teaching gives a meaning to those letter shapes.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage to whom the report of the children's teaching is brought

terms.meaning: The house of study where Sages and students learned Torah together.
Several Hebrew letters (mem, nun, tzadi, peh, kaf) are written in one shape in the middle of a word and another at the end.
The life after this one, where the righteous are rewarded.

flag: The children's letter interpretations continue past the last STORY segment (shin and tav follow in the AFTER segments), so the story stops mid-list.

note: Rabbi Yosei tells of his father, Ḥalafta, who visited Rabban Gamliel in Tiberias and found him at the table of Yoḥanan HaNazuf, reading an Aramaic translation of the book of Job. Yoḥanan told Rabban Gamliel he remembered his grandfather, also Rabban Gamliel, standing on a step on the Temple Mount when a translated Job was brought to him; he told the builder to bury it under a row of bricks. Hearing this, Rabban Gamliel ordered the book buried. Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says a bowl of mortar was turned over on it, but Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi objects: where would mortar come from on the Temple Mount, and may one destroy such writings by hand? Rather, they are left in a neglected place to decay.
why: Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda disagree whether holy books in translation may be rescued from a fire on Shabbat. Rav Huna says early Sages already disagreed, and Rabbi Yosei, who says they are not rescued, tells this incident.

note: Rav Yosef asked Rav Yosef son of Rabba which mitzva his father had been most careful about. He answered: the ritual fringes. One day, climbing the stairs, his father had a string of his fringes snap, and he would not go down until a new string was put on. Then other Sages name deeds they hope to be rewarded for. Abaye makes a feast for the Sages when a young scholar finishes a tractate. Rava does not go to sleep before searching out every argument in favor of a young scholar who comes before him for judgment. Mar bar Rav Ashi disqualifies himself from judging a young scholar, because he loves him like himself, and no one sees his own faults.
why: The Gemara is collecting sayings in which Sages name the mitzva they kept best and hope to be rewarded for; Rav Naḥman has just boasted of his fringes, and Rabba's fringes and these further boasts continue the list.

note: A certain eunuch, an apostate, taunted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa, who was bald, by asking how far it was to 'Karḥina', a pun on baldness. The rabbi answered with a pun on castration, and they traded jibes about a bald buck and a castrated goat. Seeing the rabbi without shoes, the eunuch said a man with no horse, no donkey and no shoes is worse off than the buried dead. The rabbi replied that the glory of a face is a beard, the joy of the heart is a wife, and children are God's portion, and blessed is God who denied the eunuch all three. The eunuch asked: does a bald man quarrel? The rabbi asked: does a castrated goat rebuke?
why: The Gemara is expounding Ecclesiastes' verses on old age and has quoted the Sages' sayings about aging bodies; it adds this exchange of insults about bodily defects before returning to old age.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa
people.about: A bald Sage, taunted by the eunuch, who gives as good as he gets
